big: A company books a big profit this quarter from selling land. Next quarter, the land is gone. Not all profit is equal. Some repeats, some is a one-off. Quality of earnings is how you tell them apart.

lines: Ask why. An exceptional item, like a land sale, will not repeat. Accruals book a sale before cash arrives. Receivable days show how long customers take to pay. And an auditor's qualification says something is wrong with the accounts or the audit.

q: A company books a large profit from selling land this quarter. What is this?
why: It is not core operating cash. It does not answer what was asked.
A land sale is not recurring. The details here point elsewhere.
A liability is owed money. That does not match this case.
It is an unusual gain not expected to repeat.

q: A firm books a sale in March but the customer pays in June. What is this?
why: A capital call is an AIF demand. The details here point elsewhere.
Accruals are recorded when earned, not when cash moves.
Cash arrives in June. It does not fit the facts given.
A dividend is a payout. It does not answer what was asked.

q: Customers who used to pay in 45 days now take 90. What does this show?
why: Slower payment does not double profit.
Debt is unaffected. It does not fit the facts given.
Slow collection raises doubt, not a guarantee.

q: The audit report says the auditor could not verify a large loan to a related firm. What is this?
why: It is a remark that the accounts have a problem or the audit was limited.
A clean audit has no such remark. It does not answer what was asked.
A dividend notice is unrelated. The details here point elsewhere.
A rating upgrade is unrelated. That does not match this case.

pts: Exceptional items are one-offs, not repeatable earnings.
Accruals record income when earned, not when cash moves.
Watch receivable days and auditor's qualifications.
